questions.prompt: Why can the same source give a warning with a newer compiler but become an error when the target switches to Swift 6 language mode?
questions.scenario: A mutable global warns under Swift 5 complete concurrency checking and fails under Swift 6. A teammate says the Xcode upgrade alone finished the migration.
questions.androidBridge: Compare compiler capability, Kotlin language compatibility, Gradle tooling and Android API levels as separate inputs; no numeric version mapping is implied.
rubric: Separates compiler version from the target’s Swift language mode.
Explains complete checking as a way to surface Swift 5 migration warnings.
Finds the mutable global’s missing isolation owner.
Separates package tools version, default isolation and API availability.
Limits the evidence to diagnostics rather than claiming a runtime race was demonstrated.
questions.answerHTML:
The compiler is the tool; language mode is a selected set of rules. One newer compiler can compile several modes. Swift 5 compatibility with complete concurrency checking can surface migration warnings, while Swift 6 makes race-safety violations language errors. The package tools-version header sets manifest APIs and minimum tooling; it is not sufficient evidence of every target's language mode. Record the consuming target's flags rather than inferring them from Xcode's version.

The global counter has no isolation owner: nothing defines which actor may access its mutable state. Choose MainActor for UI-owned state, an actor for independently owned state, or an immutable constant if mutation is unnecessary. Merely lowering a historical checking setting is not a Swift 6 repair. Default MainActor inference and NonisolatedNonsendingByDefault are additional module settings that should be reviewed separately. Their behavior can change even when diagnostics improve.

The companion uses explicit compiler commands to check the warning and rejection. That evidence covers diagnostics. It does not demonstrate a running race or a migrated client. Kotlin's compatibility settings and Android API requirements encourage the same input separation, but neither supplies identical checking rules. A defensible migration report names tested compiler/mode pairs and leaves target, runtime and adoption evidence pending.
followUps: How would you migrate a dependency leaf before switching the app target?
Which recorded compiler invocation proves the effective mode rather than just the declared Tuist setting?
pitfalls: Assuming a newer compiler enforces Swift 6 across every app target.
Adding unchecked annotations without deciding who owns the mutable global.

questions.prompt: How would you roll out caller-isolated async execution while keeping expensive parsing from delaying the UI?
questions.scenario: A UI module enables MainActor inference and NonisolatedNonsendingByDefault. A formerly nonisolated parser compiles cleanly, but its synchronous decode can now run on the UI actor.
questions.androidBridge: withContext(Dispatchers.Default) is an execution-policy analogy; @concurrent neither selects a Kotlin dispatcher nor promises a dedicated thread.
rubric: Treats language checking, default isolation and execution settings as separate choices.
Finds expensive synchronous work before suspension as a responsiveness risk.
Defines an explicit concurrent boundary with Sendable inputs and outputs.
Keeps cancellation and old-result rejection intact.
Names representative target checks, one accountable owner and independently reversible settings.
questions.answerHTML:
Choose three settings separately: language safety checking, default actor isolation and where an async helper executes. A clean compiler result does not prove smooth frames. Safe caller-isolated execution can still put expensive parsing on MainActor and delay other UI work. Async permits suspension; it does not itself move synchronous work away from that actor. First inventory callers and identify whether the parser is a UI-only helper or a reusable computation service.

For expensive computation, pass snapshots that satisfy Sendable and use an explicit @concurrent function. Sendable concerns safe transfer; async and throws separately describe suspension and failure. Preserve thrown failures and cancellation checks between meaningful chunks, then commit results in the owning actor with the existing generation guard. Moving an unsafe shared mutable parser off the actor would recreate the race the compiler is rejecting. A caller-isolated helper remains appropriate for short work that intentionally accesses actor-owned state.

Assign a module owner, stage a leaf change, retain the diagnostic matrix, and plan representative target recordings before making responsiveness claims. Roll back the execution feature independently from Swift 6 checking if semantics require it. Host diagnostics check the declared boundary; they cannot establish device frame timing, binary compatibility or cross-team adoption. Kotlin dispatcher selection helps explain intent but does not define Swift executor details.
followUps: Which intervals would separate parsing time from time spent waiting for the network?
What public annotations need review if default MainActor changes inferred API isolation?
pitfalls: Expecting @concurrent to make shared mutable captures safe.
Reporting host test duration as measured UI frame timing.

questions.prompt: How can an actor accept a fresh mutable Draft through sending without making Draft Sendable? What may the caller use afterward?
questions.scenario: Install accepts sending Draft. The caller creates and transfers one Draft, then asks the actor for an optional String snapshot.
questions.androidBridge: A Kotlin val freezes an alias assignment, not its object; Java 11 has no equivalent checked isolation-region transfer.
rubric: Explains the disconnected isolation region and every alias that reaches it.
Separates one sending transfer from a general Sendable contract.
Identifies source-region use that is forbidden after transfer.
Returns an optional String snapshot that is Sendable.
Separates isolation transfer from consuming ownership and deep copying.
questions.answerHTML:
Sending permits a handoff when the argument’s isolation region can safely move to another owner. Think of giving away the only usable set of keys, including aliases that reach the same state. A freshly constructed Draft can be disconnected from concurrently accessible state, so the actor can become its mutation owner. Draft remains a non-Sendable mutable class. Nothing in this handoff authorizes concurrent access to the original reference or automatically deep-copies its children.

After transfer, the caller must stop using that region through any alias. Asking the actor for an optional String returns a Sendable snapshot rather than the retained mutable object. The diagnostic fixture adds source access after install and verifies rejection; the host test follows only the valid handoff. If the screen needs continued editing, construct independent value data before transfer.

Consuming describes an ownership calling convention. Sending describes isolation transfer. They are different rules, especially when copyable aliases exist. A canceled sender cannot reclaim an already accepted region by reading the old binding. Define acceptance and reset under the receiving actor. Kotlin and Java mutable-reference behavior provide useful motivation, but their ordinary parameter calls do not enforce this Swift contract.
followUps: What if Draft contains a mutable child already reachable from another owner?
How does a sending result factory differ from returning a value with a Sendable contract?
pitfalls: Assuming sending adds lasting Sendable conformance to Draft.
Treating a let alias or shallow wrapper as proof that all reachable state is disconnected.

questions.prompt: Why can a Row’s MainActor-isolated Caption conformance work in UI code but fail in a concurrent generic renderer?
questions.scenario: Row declares @MainActor Caption. UI calls work, but an @concurrent renderer requiring Caption & Sendable is rejected. A legacy dependency proposes assumeIsolated.
questions.androidBridge: A UI-thread convention on a Java interface is weaker than Swift's isolated witness contract; dispatching is an alternative API design, not witness erasure.
rubric: Separates the instance’s Sendable capability from where its conformance may be used.
Explains why an isolated protocol witness requires the same actor domain.
Proposes a pure CaptionSnapshot with Sendable fields and nonisolated conformance.
Explains legacy checking markers without claiming they synchronize access.
Names compiler availability, adapter ownership and regression checks.
questions.answerHTML:
Passing a reference safely and calling its protocol methods safely are different permissions. Safely carrying a main-actor-isolated reference does not permit invoking its synchronous protocol implementation, called a witness, from any domain. @MainActor Caption restricts where the conformance can be used, so the concurrent generic requirement needs a nonisolated conformance that Row does not supply.

Keep the UI implementation on MainActor. For the renderer, return a CaptionSnapshot with immutable Sendable fields and a caption implementation that needs no actor-owned state. Alternatively change the consuming API to be actor-isolated if UI confinement is the actual contract. Both choices are explicit ownership designs. assumeIsolated would replace a static contract with a runtime assumption and requires justified caller evidence; it is not a general fix.

This isolated-conformance syntax needs a Swift 6.2-capable compiler. That requirement is separate from the deployed OS’s API availability. Verify valid and invalid consuming cases with the settings matrix and review imported protocol annotations. @preconcurrency import can stage legacy checking, but does not synchronize the dependency or verify queue affinity. Assign the adapter owner and retain a bounded removal plan before introducing any unchecked assertions.
followUps: When should the whole protocol require an actor rather than only one conformance?
How can another module’s default MainActor setting change a snapshot’s inferred isolation?
pitfalls: Assuming Sendable permits every protocol method to run nonisolated.
Adding assumeIsolated or @preconcurrency without proving and owning the assumption.

questions.prompt: Which trace value do async let, Task and Task.detached see? What happens when a nested task-local binding ends?
questions.scenario: Inside a trace binding, code starts async let, Task and Task.detached and joins every handle. A nested binding temporarily replaces the trace.
questions.androidBridge: Kotlin CoroutineContext is a scoped-metadata analogy; Java ThreadLocal alone does not follow suspension across thread changes.
rubric: Predicts the bound trace for the structured child and ordinary Task.
Predicts the default value for Task.detached.
Explains restoration after nested and outer scopes.
Separates inherited metadata from structured lifetime and cancellation.
Uses Sendable metadata and explicitly rebinds it in detached work when intended.
questions.answerHTML:
Task-local values are scoped labels carried with task execution. The async-let child and ordinary Task see the trace label in effect when they are created. Task.detached observes the default nil unless code explicitly supplies and rebinds an allowed value. A nested withValue binding temporarily shadows the trace, restores the outer binding on exit, and leaves the original default outside the outer scope. Suspension does not tie these values to one thread.

An ordinary Task is still unstructured: its lifetime does not become a structured child merely because it inherits the trace. Inheriting a trace, actor context or priority does not make its lifetime a structured child or guarantee cancellation when the creating task is canceled. Join or otherwise own its handle. An inherited value may remain in that independent task after the lexical binding scope ends.

Use immutable Sendable metadata for the trace. A task-local wrapper does not make a shared mutable account object safe. If detached work intentionally correlates with the request, capture the permitted value and bind it within the detached scope; also specify its independent shutdown owner. The companion confirms the bounded inheritance/restoration observations. Kotlin context elements offer similar motivation but have their own propagation APIs and cancellation semantics.
followUps: What continues if you drop an ordinary Task handle before completion?
Why is a shared mutable object unsafe as trace metadata without its own isolation contract?
pitfalls: Treating task-local values as tied to one thread.
Expecting inherited metadata to imply automatic parent cancellation.

questions.prompt: For a slow consumer, what does channel send completion prove? Define demand, processing acknowledgment and cancellation.
questions.scenario: A producer sends commands that the consumer saves. The engineer treats returned AsyncChannel.send as proof of saving and starts one task per command.
questions.androidBridge: Kotlin rendezvous channels illustrate demand, but canceled-send exceptions and close semantics differ from AsyncChannel's nonthrowing send.
rubric: Separates receipt of a command from completion of its processing.
Bounds producer count, pending elements and payload size.
Explains that cancellation or finish can unblock send without delivery.
Defines a separate bounded acknowledgment for completed processing.
Uses registration barriers and an injected clock to test ordering and timeout.
Names producer and consumer shutdown owners and recovery behavior.
questions.answerHTML:
A channel handing over a command is like a clerk accepting a form. It does not mean the form has been saved. AsyncChannel.send waits for iteration consumption but can also unblock on cancellation or termination, so normal return alone cannot certify database commit. Use an explicit command identity and a separately owned acknowledgment if persistence completion is required. Bound outstanding acknowledgments and resolve them on failure or shutdown.

Starting one task per command can leave unlimited suspended producers, each still holding its payload. A small buffer alone does not bound that memory. Bound active producers and payload sizes as well as accepted buffering. The companion instead uses a zero-buffer channel with one pending sender and receiver, rejecting overlapping blocked operations. Its throwing cancellation/closed policy is deliberately narrower than AsyncChannel's API.

Name the producer owner that finishes the channel and joins its tasks when the consumer exits. Preserve ordinary failure, cancellation and intentional end-of-input as distinct outcomes. Test registered sender cancellation, registered receiver cancellation, replacement delivery and idempotent finish with event barriers. Inject Clock for timeout policy rather than guessing wall-clock scheduling. Host tests establish those local transitions; a pinned library integration and persistence recovery need their own evidence.
followUps: Which outcome wins if a sender and receiver match before cancellation is processed?
How would the acknowledgment distinguish receipt from a committed save?
pitfalls: Reporting consumer processing as complete merely because send returned.
Claiming zero buffering bounds unlimited suspended producer tasks.

questions.prompt: How should OwnedInt initialize and release its allocated slot? Why is reading the owner after consuming extract rejected?
questions.scenario: OwnedInt allocates and initializes one Int. It offers borrowing read and consuming extract, then deinitializes and deallocates in deinit. A reviewer wants to read it again after extract.
questions.androidBridge: AutoCloseable and Kotlin use express cleanup scopes but generally allow aliasing; they do not give Java 11 Swift's consumed-binding rule.
rubric: Separates reserving storage from initializing a value in it.
Ends the value lifetime and uses the matching deallocation operation.
Explains borrowing access versus consuming self.
Rejects reuse of the consumed binding.
Keeps noncopyability separate from Sendable and correctness of unsafe internals.
questions.answerHTML:
Allocation reserves room for one Int. Initialize puts a live Int value in that room. Empty storage and an initialized value are different states. Deinit must end that value lifetime before releasing the storage with the matching Swift allocator operation. A borrowed read accesses the owner without destroying or transferring it. Consuming extract takes self, returns an independent Int, and ends the caller's ability to reuse the owner.

Extract consumes the owner, so the caller cannot read that binding afterward. The compiler fixture checks that rejection. This is distinct from inout exclusivity, which forbids overlapping conflicting accesses even when a program uses a single thread. It is also distinct from sending, which concerns isolation-region transfer rather than the ownership calling convention.

Noncopyable prevents certain accidental copies of the owner. It cannot repair an incorrect deinitializer, an address kept beyond its lifetime or a read outside the allocation. It does not grant Sendable to unsafe storage. Keep the pointer private, return values rather than borrowed addresses, and check cancellation before allocating where practical. Native-resource cleanup can need asynchronous shutdown acknowledgment beyond synchronous deinit. The package verifies the bounded values and diagnostic boundaries, leaving unsafe ABI and sanitizer audits separate.
followUps: How must cleanup account for only part of a buffer being initialized?
Why does noncopyable ownership alone not make the resource safe across executors?
pitfalls: Using Swift deallocate for memory owned by a different C allocator.
Treating ~Copyable as complete memory-safety or concurrency-safety proof.

questions.prompt: Who retains a C callback context, and when may cancellation release it if callbacks can repeat until unregister confirms they have stopped?
questions.scenario: A C registration stores an opaque pointer to CallbackBox. Completion races cancellation. Callbacks can repeat until unregister acknowledges that no callback is active or can start.
questions.androidBridge: JNI global-reference and listener-registration lifetimes offer motivation; their release APIs are not interchangeable with Unmanaged retain operations.
rubric: Gives the registration one retain and each callback only borrowed access.
Separates retained ownership operations from unretained reconstruction.
Waits for confirmed callback quiescence before final release.
Names exactly one release owner across completion and cancellation.
Keeps callback errors, canceled waiting and completed shutdown distinct.
Limits the synchronous sample claim and requires evidence for the real foreign API.
questions.answerHTML:
The registration keeps one retained context alive until callbacks have stopped. Each callback borrows that same context, like using a key that must stay available for the whole registration. Each callback reconstructs the documented object type and borrows it while that registration ownership remains valid. Consuming the sole +1 with takeRetainedValue on the first callback would leave later callbacks without that ownership. Conversely, never balancing the registration retain leaks the box.

Cancellation must request unregister and wait for the C API’s guarantee that no callback is running or can start. That state is quiescence. Only then may the final release occur. Setting a Swift task's cancellation flag or removing a UI owner is insufficient. Define a state machine in which exactly one terminal path owns release, and completion/cancellation messages cannot release twice. Keep ordinary callback failure, canceled waiting and successful shutdown distinct.

The companion uses passRetained and takeRetainedValue in one synchronous, one-shot round trip; its weak observation verifies only that local retain balance. Do not present it as proof that a real C API unregisters safely. Assign an adapter owner, cite the vendor's callback/lifetime contract, and test controlled repeated-callback and shutdown schedules in an appropriate target before shipping. Prefer a copied Sendable result at the Swift boundary.
followUps: Who keeps the context alive if unregister returns before an active callback finishes?
How could a truly one-shot callback consume its retained context differently?
pitfalls: Releasing the context immediately on Task.cancel.
Consuming the registration’s one retain independently in every repeated callback.
